# Knowledge tracing {#knowledge-tracing}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain how **Bayesian knowledge tracing** (BKT) follows a student's
  mastery of a skill from one practice attempt to the next, and what its
  four parameters mean;
* fit BKT to practice logs with `mv_kt_fit()`, including the variants
  with forgetting and with a guess and a slip per item, and judge the
  models by cross-validation with `mv_kt_cv()`;
* compare BKT with a Rasch model on the same logs with `mv_kt_irt()`, and
  relate BKT's guess parameters to IRT item difficulty;
* draw mastery over time and on a knowledge graph with `gg_kt()`, and
  check a graph's prerequisites against practice logs with
  `mv_kt_prereq()`.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[Knowledge tracing](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#knowledge-tracing),
[knowledge graph](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#knowledge-graph),
[attribute hierarchy](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#attribute-hierarchy),
[cross-validation](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#cross-validation),
[likelihood-ratio test](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#likelihood-ratio-test).

The functions in this chapter are experimental: Their arguments and
output may still change.

## The ideas

IRT assumes that a student's ability stays the same while they answer the
test. That is reasonable for a one-hour exam, but not for an online tutor,
where students practise a skill until they get it. In practice logs, the
interesting question is not how able a student is, but whether they have
learned the skill yet, and when.

**Bayesian knowledge tracing** [@corbett1995] answers it with a hidden
Markov model. Each skill is either **known** or **not known**. Four
probabilities describe each skill:

* `prior`: The probability that a student knows the skill before the
  first attempt;
* `learn`: The probability that a student who does not know the skill
  learns it after an attempt (with feedback);
* `guess`: The probability of a correct answer without knowing the skill;
* `slip`: The probability of a wrong answer while knowing it.

After every answer, Bayes' rule updates the probability that the student
knows the skill. A correct answer raises it, a wrong one lowers it, and
then the chance of learning moves it up before the next attempt:

$$
P(L_t \mid \text{correct}) = \frac{P(L_t)(1 - S)}{P(L_t)(1 - S) + (1 - P(L_t))G}, \qquad
P(L_{t+1}) = P(L_t \mid \text{answer}) + (1 - P(L_t \mid \text{answer}))\,T,
$$

where $S$ is the slip, $G$ the guess and $T$ the learn rate. The
parameters are estimated by expectation-maximization, skill by skill, as
the pyBKT library does [@badrinath2021]. Bulut et al.
[-@bulut2023bkt] introduce BKT with pyBKT for psychometricians; this
chapter follows their examples in R.

BKT and IRT are close relatives [@deonovic2018]. The guess parameter of a
skill, or of an item when each item has its own (the item difficulty
effect model, KT-IDEM; @pardos2011), plays the role of item difficulty:
Items that are easy to answer without knowing the skill are easy items.
What BKT adds is learning: The latent state changes during the logs.

## Example 1: Plotting skills in a Cognitive Tutor

```{r data-knowledge-tracing-1}
logs <- cognitive_tutor
```

`cognitive_tutor` holds the practice logs used in the pyBKT examples
[@stamper2010]: 587 students' first attempts at 16,857 problem steps in a
mathematics tutor, each tagged with one of 12 skills. Following Bulut et
al. [-@bulut2023bkt], we start with the six skills about plotting numbers
on a number line.

```{r}
head(logs)
plot_skills <- grep("^Plot", unique(logs$skill), value = TRUE)
kt <- mv_kt_fit(logs, skills = plot_skills, seed = 1)
kt
```

The parameters tell a story about each skill. Plotting whole numbers is
known by almost everyone from the start (`prior` 0.93), so the model has
little to learn from these logs; its guess reaches the upper bound of 0.5
that keeps known and not-known students apart. Plotting pi is learned
quickly (`learn` 0.62), and plotting terminating proper fractions slowly
(0.03), with a high slip: Students who probably know it still make many
mistakes. A skill with a guess of 0 and a slip of 0.31, such as plotting
non-terminating improper fractions, says that a correct answer is strong
evidence of knowing the skill but a wrong one is weak evidence of not
knowing it.

```{r kt-curves, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Learning curves for the plotting skills: The mean probability of knowing each skill before each attempt (lines) and the proportion of correct answers (points)."}
gg_kt(kt, max_attempts = 15)
```

One student's record shows the updating at work.

```{r kt-student, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "One student's probability of knowing each plotting skill after every attempt: Filled points are correct answers."}
student <- names(which.max(table(logs$student[logs$skill %in% plot_skills])))
gg_kt(kt, student = student)
```

### Variants

pyBKT's two most used variants are available as arguments: `forgets =
TRUE` lets a known skill be forgotten, and `multigs = TRUE` gives each item
(here each problem) its own guess and slip.

```{r}
kt_f <- mv_kt_fit(logs, skills = plot_skills, forgets = TRUE, seed = 1)
kt_g <- mv_kt_fit(logs, item = "problem", skills = plot_skills, multigs = TRUE, seed = 1)
rbind(standard = glance(kt), forgets = glance(kt_f), multigs = glance(kt_g))
```

Forgetting adds nothing here: The log-likelihood barely moves and AIC goes
up. Item guess and slip fit much better (AIC drops by more than 100 and
the AUC rises from 0.75 to 0.81), but they add 184 parameters, and BIC
prefers the standard model. Fit on the same logs always flatters the
bigger model, so the fair test is new students.

```{r}
cv <- mv_kt_cv(logs, skills = plot_skills, folds = 3, seed = 1)
cv_g <- mv_kt_cv(logs, item = "problem", skills = plot_skills, multigs = TRUE,
                 folds = 3, seed = 1)
merge(cv[cv$fold == "mean", c("skill", "rmse", "auc")],
      cv_g[cv_g$fold == "mean", c("skill", "rmse", "auc")],
      by = "skill", suffixes = c("_standard", "_multigs"))
```

On held-out students the item model still predicts better for most skills,
especially the ones with many problems, such as plotting terminating
proper fractions. The cross-validated RMSE of the standard model (0.29 for
plotting whole numbers, 0.46 for plotting pi) is close to what Bulut et
al. [-@bulut2023bkt] report from pyBKT.

## Example 2: Knowledge tracing and IRT

How does BKT compare with an IRT model on the same logs? `mv_kt_irt()`
holds out the last 30% of each student's attempts on each skill, fits both
models to the rest, and forecasts the held-out answers. The IRT model is a
Rasch model with crossed random effects for students and items, fitted
with lme4.

```{r}
cmp <- mv_kt_irt(logs, item = "problem", skills = plot_skills, seed = 1)
cmp
tidy(cmp)
```

The two models forecast about equally well. BKT ranks the answers a
little better on average (a mean AUC of 0.76 against 0.72), because it
updates after every answer, while IRT keeps each student's ability fixed.
IRT has the lower RMSE and the higher accuracy for three of the skills, because its item
difficulties capture differences between problems that the standard BKT
model ignores. Neither model is right: Students learn and items differ,
and each model captures one of the two.

The second half of the output connects the parameters.

```{r}
tidy(cmp, "items")
```

For every skill, the IRT difficulty of a problem is strongly correlated
with the log of its BKT guess, with a median of about -0.89: The easier
the problem, the more often students who do not know the skill still get
it right. Bulut et al. [-@bulut2023bkt] report correlations between 0.55
and 0.94 (in absolute value) for the same skills. When item guess and
slip are estimated, BKT's guess parameter is an item difficulty in
disguise.

## Example 3: Practice on a knowledge graph

Chapter \@ref(knowledge-graphs) described the Grade 5 fractions test as a
knowledge graph. `fractions_logs` holds simulated practice logs on the same
items: 400 students practise the six concepts in blocks, mostly in the
curriculum order, until they answer three in a row correctly.

```{r data-knowledge-tracing-2}
practice <- fractions_logs
kg <- fractions_kg
```

The logs have no skill column. With `kg`, `mv_kt_fit()` maps each item to
the concepts it measures in the graph.

```{r}
head(practice)
kt_fr <- mv_kt_fit(practice, kg = kg, seed = 1)
kt_fr
```

```{r kt-graph, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "The fractions graph shaded by the mean probability of knowing each concept after the last practice attempt."}
gg_kt(kt_fr, type = "graph")
```

The graph view shows where the class stands: Nearly everyone has fraction
meaning, and adding and subtracting is the least secure. For one student,
`gg_kt(kt_fr, student = "P001", type = "graph")` gives the same picture, a
diagnostic report that follows the graph.

### Checking prerequisites against the logs

A prerequisite is a claim about learning: A student who does not know
equivalent fractions should struggle to learn to add fractions with
unlike denominators. Practice logs can test that claim directly.
`mv_kt_prereq()` estimates, for every pair of concepts A and B, the learn
rate of B on the attempts made while A was probably known and on those
made while it was not, and tests the difference with a likelihood ratio
test. Each test uses only the attempts where B's other prerequisites in the
graph are already known, so an indirect prerequisite adds little.

```{r}
check <- mv_kt_prereq(kt_fr)
check
head(tidy(check)[, c("from", "to", "edge", "learn_without", "learn_with", "ratio", "lr", "verdict")], 8)
```

All five prerequisites of the graph are supported: Each concept is learned
three to eight times as fast once its prerequisite is known. The
strongest effect in the logs, though, is not in the graph: Comparing
fractions is learned ten times as fast once equivalent fractions are
known. This is the edge the published graph misses, the same one that
`mv_kg_fit()` found in the test answers in Chapter
\@ref(knowledge-graphs). Two independent kinds of evidence, a test taken
once and practice over time, point to the same repair.

```{r}
kg2 <- mv_kg_edit(kg, add = data.frame(from = "equivalent", to = "compare"))
mv_kt_prereq(kt_fr, kg = kg2)
```

With the edge added, the logs agree with the graph. Practice logs have one
more advantage over a test: The direction of a prerequisite is in the
data. Equivalent fractions speed up learning to compare, and not the other
way round, so no assumption about which concept is easier is needed.

The learn rates of the first model also make sense now. They are lower
than the rates the logs were simulated with (for example 0.12 against 0.20
for comparing fractions), because some students practised a concept before
its prerequisites and learned it slowly. A single learn rate per skill
averages over both groups; the graph explains why learning is uneven.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Fit the standard model to all 12 skills of `cognitive_tutor`. Which
   skill has the lowest learn rate, and what would you tell the tutor's
   designers about it?
2. Refit the plotting skills with both `forgets = TRUE` and `multigs =
   TRUE`. Does forgetting help once items have their own guess and slip?
3. Run `mv_kt_irt()` on the three "Finding the intersection" skills. Which
   model forecasts better, and why might that be?
4. Add a wrong prerequisite, `mixed -> compare`, to the fractions graph
   (together with `equivalent -> compare`) and run `mv_kt_prereq()`. What
   does it report?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
# 1. all skills
kt_all <- mv_kt_fit(logs, seed = 1)
p <- tidy(kt_all)
p[order(p$learn), c("skill", "prior", "learn", "guess", "slip")][1:3, ]

# 2. both variants
kt_fg <- mv_kt_fit(logs, item = "problem", skills = plot_skills, multigs = TRUE,
                   forgets = TRUE, seed = 1)
rbind(multigs = glance(kt_g), both = glance(kt_fg))

# 3. intersection skills
inter <- grep("^Finding", unique(logs$skill), value = TRUE)
mv_kt_irt(logs, item = "problem", skills = inter, seed = 1)

# 4. a wrong prerequisite
kg3 <- mv_kg_edit(kg, add = data.frame(from = c("equivalent", "mixed"),
                                       to = c("compare", "compare")))
mv_kt_prereq(kt_fr, kg = kg3)
```

1. Plotting terminating proper fractions has the lowest learn rate (about
   0.03): Students barely improve with practice. The designers should look
   at the feedback and hints for this skill, or split it into smaller
   skills; it may also be two skills tagged as one, which BKT would see as
   slow learning with many slips.
2. No: The log-likelihood is the same and AIC rises. Wrong answers by
   students who seemed to know a skill are explained by item slips, not by
   forgetting.
3. IRT forecasts better for these skills. Each has few students (about 70)
   and items that differ a lot in difficulty, which the Rasch model
   captures and the standard BKT model does not; with sparse sequences
   there is also little learning for BKT to track.
4. It flags `mixed -> compare` as a weak prerequisite: Comparing fractions
   is learned just as fast whether or not a student knows mixed numbers.
   The check works in both directions, finding missing edges and
   questioning ones that are there.

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Corbett and Anderson [-@corbett1995] introduced knowledge tracing in the
ACT Programming Tutor. Badrinath, Wang and Pardos [-@badrinath2021]
describe pyBKT and its variants, and Bulut et al. [-@bulut2023bkt]
introduce BKT for readers who know IRT, with the examples this chapter
follows. Pardos and Heffernan [-@pardos2011] add item difficulty to
knowledge tracing, and Deonovic et al. [-@deonovic2018] work out the
formal relation between BKT and IRT. Deep knowledge tracing [@piech2015]
replaces the hidden Markov model with a recurrent neural network; it
needs much larger logs, and its predictions are harder to interpret.
